Newborn Southern multimammate mice enter the world at a remarkably diminutive size, with individuals typically weighing just 2.0 grams [Wwb = 2.0 grams] at birth. This altricial neonate is entirely dependent on maternal care and thermoregulation, a common pattern among murid rodents where substantial post-natal investment is necessary for survival. Gestation in this species lasts a precisely measured 23 days [tg = 23 days] when females are maintained at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This relatively short gestation is consistent with the species’ high fecundity, allowing females to produce multiple litters within a single breeding season. The combination of a low birth weight and a rapid gestation appears to be a life-history strategy that prioritizes high reproductive output over substantial per-offspring investment. Such a strategy is typical of small-bodied rodents inhabiting unpredictable environments, where the ability to quickly replace generations can be a key determinant of population persistence.

As the suckling juvenile progresses through its early development, the dependency on maternal milk ends at a characteristic age. Weaning occurs when the offspring reaches 21 days after birth [tx = 21 days after birth], marking the transition to solid food and nutritional independence at a temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This milestone is reached under the same controlled thermal regime of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], which facilitates efficient metabolic processing during this critical dietary switch. Following this, the young animals enter a sub-adult phase characterized by rapid somatic growth and the accumulation of body reserves. They continue to develop until reaching their ultimate asymptotic body mass. For adult Mastomys coucha, the ultimate wet weight, or the maximum body mass attained by fully grown individuals, has been recorded at 36 grams [Wwi = 36 grams]. This relatively modest adult size influences a range of ecological traits, from predator vulnerability to daily caloric requirements.

Female Mastomys coucha undergo a well-defined developmental trajectory to reach reproductive competence. The time since birth at which puberty occurs, marking the onset of gonadal activity and the ability to ovulate, has been observed at 112 days after birth [tp = 112 days after birth] at a temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This measurement was obtained from individuals housed at a steady ambient temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], a condition that likely aligns with the species’ thermoneutral zone and supports normal endocrine function. Reaching this stage signifies that the female is now capable of breeding, although first reproduction may be further influenced by social cues and nutritional status. This comparatively early age at maturation allows for rapid population turnover, a characteristic feature of r-selected species adapted to fluctuating or disturbed habitats. The attainment of sexual maturity thus represents a key transition, enabling females to begin contributing to the next generation within their first year of life.

One of the most striking life-history attributes of the Southern multimammate mouse is its extraordinary reproductive capacity. Captive studies have documented that a female can produce an average of 3.9 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3.9 pups per litter]. When combined with their short inter-birth intervals, this results in a very high overall output. Under stable environmental conditions kept at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], these females are capable of achieving a maximal reproductive frequency of approximately 12 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 12 litters per year]. This impressive frequency is a direct consequence of the accelerated life-history described previously: a brief gestation coupled with an early weaning age allows females to be nearly continuously pregnant. This remarkable fecundity helps explain the species’ reputation as a significant agricultural pest in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, where populations can irrupt explosively following favorable rains and cause extensive crop damage.

Despite its high reproductive output, the lifespan of Mastomys coucha is not indefinite, and individuals are subject to the typical constraints of senescence. The maximum recorded longevity for this species, observed under ideal captive conditions free from predation and disease, is 4 years [am = 4 years] at a temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This value was documented at a constant temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This relatively short lifespan is congruent with its rapid maturation and high fecundity, placing it firmly on the fast end of the slow-fast continuum of life-history strategies. In natural settings, however, actual longevity is likely much shorter due to extrinsic mortality factors. The interplay between a high daily reproductive rate and a brief potential lifespan creates a demographic profile where populations are highly dynamic, capable of both rapid growth and sudden declines. This species thus serves as an excellent model for understanding how small mammals balance the trade-offs between current reproduction and future survival in variable environments.
